item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] As heavy rains swamp Gaza's tents, Israel must face sanctions
item.description:
As heavy rains swamp Gaza's tents, Israel must face sanctions

Submitted by Chris Doyle on Mon, 11/09/2026 - 20:03
The world cannot sit idly by as the Netanyahu regime, withholding vital supplies, imposes mass collective punishment
A displaced Palestinian boy stands at the entrance to his flooded tent as he looks at a water puddle after heavy rainfall in Gaza City's Al-Remal neighbourhood on 7 November, 2026 (AFP)
Off

It took a mere dozen hours of the first winter storm to flood around 70,000 tents in Gaza. Even 1,000 would be worthy of major humanitarian action, but just imagine that multiplied by 70.

These devastating floods were predicted and predictable. Nothing about this should surprise anyone who has paid even the scantest attention to the humanitarian situation in Gaza. 

Every year, Palestinians in the coastal enclave face the threat of flooding due to winter rains. Years ago, it was already challenging enough, as raw sewage flooded the streets, fuelling the spread of disease.

Israel’s blockade of Gaza, in place for two decades, along with periodic military bombardments, would render these inundations particularly life-threatening. Much of the debate in years past was about the inability to pump water out, including the lack of fuel for pumps, owing to Israel’s blockade. 

In contrast to the situation in 2026, however, that was a minor crisis.

Three years into the genocide, the rains are once again life-threatening, not life-giving. This is the fourth winter many have been forced to face this challenge. 

In Gaza, 65 percent of people - more than one million - live in tents or makeshift shelters. Amid rain and high winds, they fear for their lives. 

Many tents have been washed away, along with vital possessions, while those in ruined buildings face the genuine possibility that the structures will collapse. Disease and hunger, already a daily threat, will intensify across this brutalised strip of land. 

Manmade catastrophe

This is not an accident of nature. It is a manmade catastrophe, fashioned by the Israeli leadership, with a manmade solution that is denied by the very same leadership. Israeli authorities have denied entry of vital life-saving supplies and equipment. 

Take tents. Prior to these floods, humanitarian agencies warned that many of the existing tents had worn out and were insufficient. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, 121,000 tents are needed, while only 2,800 are inside Gaza. 

Other international actors cannot remain silent and inert, which was their standard operating procedure for years, even before the genocide

Just across the border in Egypt, 150,000 tents donated for Gaza lie useless, waiting for Israel to permit them to enter. The price of tents on the market has rocketed upwards, way beyond the purchasing power of those in areas like al-Mawasi, which hosts more than 900,000 internally displaced Palestinians.

Israel has only permitted limited tents to enter. What is the great security risk of a tent? 

Then again, this is the state that denied all food, water, medicines and fuel for protracted periods of time on two occasions, leading to famine, and only easing this policy after considerable American pressure. 

Israel today occupies nearly 70 percent of the Gaza Strip, with Palestinians herded into ever-smaller, unsanitary, overcrowded hellscapes. In the past, they would have been to able to shift to safe ground. But nowhere is safe in Gaza now - and for those not following, the ceasefire announced in October 2025 is in name only. 

For Palestinians in Gaza, if the bombs don’t get them, the floods, famine and disease will. 

Taking a lead

In Israel, the governing coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to its usual blame game, saying it’s all Hamas’s fault. While the rump of the Hamas authority in Gaza has serious failings, it has barely any ability in the midst of a genocide to handle these floods. 

Israel, however, can take action - and importantly, it has an international legal obligation, as the occupying power, to care for the people in the territory it occupies. It could allow all necessary equipment into the strip, and lift its ban, which should never have been imposed, on the UN relief agency for Palestinians and three dozen other aid agencies. 

Gaza genocide: How Israel made horror a ritual of daily life
Read More »

Even the “Board of Peace”, the opaque concoction devised by the administration of US President Donald Trump to oversee the flow of aid into Gaza, described the Israeli response as “insufficient”. In a statement, it called on the Israeli government to “authorize and facilitate the entry of all necessary winterization and humanitarian supplies”. 

Other international actors cannot remain silent and inert, which was their standard operating procedure for years, even before the genocide. They cannot - and must not - defer action until the arcane process of Israeli coalition-building and political chicanery glues together the next fractious Israeli government. 

Sanctions have been, and remain, a requirement. With most other states, in the event of mass collective punishment of hundreds of thousands of civilians, a ream of ever-tightening bans and sanctions would be issued by European states. 

The United Kingdom can take a lead. It recently amended its Global Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law Sanctions Regulations to allow the UK government to sanction those who block humanitarian aid. Gaza is the perfect example of a situation where these sanctions need to be invoked, as dozens of politicians argued in a letter to Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband last month. 

Other states must adopt similar measures immediately. Thousands of Palestinian lives are at stake in a situation that can easily be relieved. 

It is time to break the terrible record of consistently failing Palestinian men, women and children, which has tarnished the international record for so long.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Why are the UAE, Sudan and Egypt fighting for influence inside Ethiopia’s Tigray state?
item.description:
Why are the UAE, Sudan and Egypt fighting for influence inside Ethiopia’s Tigray state?

Submitted by Daniel Tester on Mon, 11/09/2026 - 10:50
Gulf kingdoms and neighbouring countries are transforming the crisis into a wider battle for the Horn of Africa
An Ethiopian Federal Police patrol on 9 October 2026 after forces pushed back the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) in Mekelle (AFP)
On

Fighting has continued across the Tigray region of northern Ethiopia, after a coalition of rebel groups seized territory in September.

The government, which the insurgents have vowed to overthrow, has managed to contain much of the fighting, although explosions were heard in Addis Ababa in October.

Tigray is no stranger to conflict. Amid accusations of war crimes and genocide, hundreds of thousands of people were killed and millions more displaced during the civil war from 2020-22.

But now there are fears that the current conflict could escalate into a war between Ethiopia and neighbouring Eritrea, which it accuses of backing the rebels. The two countries severed relations in October.

The Red Sea region is already beset with war across Sudan, Yemen and Somalia.

Ethiopia has an ally in the UAE, while Eritrea can look to Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Sudan for support.

Here’s everything you need to know about Tigray, past conflicts, and the role other countries are playing.

Where is Tigray?

Tigray is Ethiopia’s northernmost state, bordering Eritrea and a small part of Sudan.  

Roughly the size of Slovakia or the US state of West Virginia, it has a population of around 7.5 million people, according to the Ethiopian government. 

The majority of the inhabitants are Tigrayan, one of the 80-plus ethnic groups in Ethiopia and make up around six percent of the overall population. 

The landscape is dominated by rocky highlands, which contain some of Ethiopia’s largest deposits of gold and other minerals.

The largest faith is Orthodox Ethiopian Christianity, as it is in the rest of Ethiopia, although a third of the country’s population is Muslim. Most Tigrayans speak Tigrinya, the most widely spoken language in Eritrea. 

Eritrea shares strong cultural roots with Tigray, but itself split from Ethiopia in 1993 after a bloody series of wars that lasted three decades and killed between 100,000 and 200,000 people.

Who are the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF)?

Politics in Tigray is dominated by the TPLF, a paramilitary group and political party founded in 1975.

It fought a war against Ethiopia’s military governments from 1975 to 1991, during which it allied with Eritrean separatists themselves fighting for independence from Ethiopia (which they formally achieved in 1993).

The conflict ended when the TPLF and other rebels overthrew the Ethiopian government.

The TPLF-led coalition established the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front, a left-wing government, that ruled for the next 27 years, overseeing economic growth and expanding public services.

But it was accused of suppressing dissent, concentrating power in the hands of Tigrayan elites and voter intimidation in elections where it often won every parliamentary seat.

The coalition also fell out with Eritrea, fighting a two-year border war over Tigray during 1998 that saw tens of thousands killed on each side. 

In 2018, Abiy Ahmed, from the Oromo, Ethiopia’s largest ethnic group, came to power after anti-government protests. The following year, as prime minister, he dissolved the government and formed the Prosperity Party, a new coalition which the TPLF refused to join. 

Ahmed also signed a peace deal with Eritrea in 2018 that officially ended the earlier conflict and for which he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

What happened during the 2020-22 civil war?

In 2020, the TPLF held its own regional elections in Tigray in defiance of Addis Ababa. 

War broke out in November 2020 when Ethiopia’s army began an offensive in Tigray, amid accusations of TPLF attacks on military bases, which the rebels denied.

Eritrean fighters and militias, particularly from the neighbouring Amhara region, fought alongside the government. 

The government blockaded imports of food, medicine and other goods into Tigray, triggering mass starvation estimated to have killed at least 200,000 people. 

Rights monitors accused all sides of war crimes and crimes against humanity, including the large-scale rape and massacre of civilians. The government and its allies were also accused of genocide against Tigrayans.

Death toll estimates range from 160,000 to over 600,000, with more than two million internally displaced, and tens of thousands more leaving the country, mostly to neighbouring Sudan. 

The war ended in November 2022 with the Pretoria Agreement, mediated by the African Union, which gave the TPLF some regional autonomy.

Why is there war in Tigray now?

Since 2022, peace in Tigray has been fragile. Many provisions of the Pretoria Agreement, including the return of displaced people and the disarmament of the TPLF, remain unimplemented. 

The TPLF has faced its own internal power struggle. In March 2025, a TPLF faction led by Debretsion Gebremichael, an opponent of aspects of the Pretoria Agreement, forced out Getachew Reda, leader of the regional administration, who fled to Addis Ababa and became an adviser to Abiy, his former enemy.  

In January clashes broke out between the TPLF and government forces in western Tigray. By July the TPLF declared the Pretoria Agreement “effectively dead”.

In September, the TPLF said it had joined with other groups, including former civil war enemies, to form the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Coalition for Survival (also known as Tsimdo).

In a joint statement, the groups said they would overthrow Abiy’s government, saying that “war, genocide, mass slaughter and absolute poverty have become its defining features”.

Tsimdo launched a military offensive on 23 September, seizing Mekelle, Tigray’s regional capital, as well as territory in the states of Afar and Amhara. 

The government retook Mekelle without a fight within weeks, with the TPLF fleeing to outposts in Tigray’s highlands. But the rebels have vowed to continue fighting. Gebremichael said on 4 October: "We will attack the enemy where we choose, not where he chooses for us."

How is Eritrea involved?

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of covertly aiding the TPLF and sending troops across the border in support in September. 

Eritrea has denied the allegations, but witnesses and conflict monitors have reported its soldiers' presence in Tigray. Following Ethiopian drone strikes, it has withdrawn some fighters from Ethiopia. 

The two states severed diplomatic ties on 1 October. Ethiopia, in a letter to the UN Security Council, accusing Eritrea of “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”.

Eritrea’s backing for the TPLF is a striking reversal from its position during the 2020-22 war, when it allied with Abiy’s government against the rebels, as well as the 1998-2000 war, when it battled a TPLF-led Ethiopia. 

Instead, the alliance harkens back to Ethiopia’s 1975-1991 civil war, the last major conflict when Eritreans and Tigrayan rebels fought together.

The move comes amid a major fallout between Ethiopia and Eritrea over Eritrea’s prized Red Sea coastline.

Ethiopia, with a population of 140 million, is the world’s largest landlocked state, having lost access to the sea when Eritrea gained independence in 1993.

In recent years, Abiy has repeatedly stated that the country needs maritime access. Many Eritreans have interpreted this as a declaration of Ethiopian intent to seize territory: Eritrea's port of Assab is just 70km from Ethiopia’s border.

What is the UAE’s involvement in Tigray? 

Abu Dhabi has strong ties with Ethiopia, where it has invested billions since Abiy came to power in 2018. Ethiopia has said the priorities are “manufacturing, food processing, agriculture, packaging, construction materials, and logistics”.

A former Ethiopian government adviser told Middle East Eye in April that “many in Ethiopia’s foreign ministry and elsewhere believe the UAE has been calling the shots in Ethiopia in regard to the Sudanese government, RSF and Eritrea over the port of Assab for at least two years”.

On 25 September, the UAE backed Abiy’s government and condemned the TPLF attacks. In the past, it has given Ethiopia military support: Emirati drones and other armaments were identified in the Ethiopian military’s arsenal during the 2020-22 war.

Both Ethiopia and the UAE want to expand their influence in the Red Sea. They have collaborated in Somaliland, the breakaway region of Somalia on Ethiopia’s eastern border where Abu Dhabi has invested billions in the Berbera seaport and Emirati military bases.

In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with Somaliland to use the facilities and to build its own naval bases in exchange for recognising Somaliland sovereignty.

But the deal angered Somalia. Ethiopia was forced to row back its ambitions for naval bases amid diplomatic mediation from Turkey, which has ties with both states. Today, most of Ethiopia’s trade still passes through neighbouring Djibouti. 

Emirati relations with Eritrea are icy. Eritrea’s foreign minister Osman Saleh accused Abu Dhabi of pursuing “port imperialism” across Africa in an exclusive interview with MEE in September.  

Is Sudan involved in Tigray?

Ethiopia has tense relations with its northern neighbour Sudan. In 2021, there were violent clashes between Ethiopians and Sudanese over the contested border area of al-Fashaga.

The two countries have since exchanged recriminations.

Ethiopian military chief Birhanu Jula accused Sudan in September of supporting the TPLF, although he gave no evidence. Khartoum called the allegation “baseless”. Ethiopia expelled six Sudanese diplomats on 4 November.

In turn, Sudan accused Ethiopia of assisting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the UAE-backed Sudanese paramilitary force which is fighting the Sudanese government and is widely accused of atrocities.

Both Ethiopia and the UAE deny backing the RSF. But their support is widely documented: analysis of satellite imagery by Yale’s Humanitarian Research Lab, revealed by Middle East Eye in April, showed strong visual evidence that RSF fighters and supplies were travelling through an Ethiopian military base in its western Benishangul-Gumuz state. 

How is Egypt involved with Tigray? 

Ethiopia, Africa’s second most populous country, and Egypt, its third, have long been regional rivals. 

Central to the tension is Ethiopia’s Grand Renaissance Dam, a $5bn megaproject inaugurated in 2025 that will lower water levels on Egypt’s downstream stretch of the River Nile, and is viewed in Cairo as a threat to national security.

The rift has only widened amid Ethiopia’s alleged support for the RSF in Sudan, where Egypt has ties to the government forces. 

In September, Jula accused Egypt of supporting the TPLF without evidence. Egypt has denied the accusation. 

The two countries expelled each other’s diplomats in October, but maintain formal relations. 

Egypt has also developed close relations with Eritrea’s leader Isaias Afwerki amid joint concerns about Ethiopia’s Red Sea ambitions. 

What about Saudi Arabia and Tigray?

The media in Ethiopia has accused Saudi Arabia, the UAE’s main regional rival, of backing the rebels in Tigray. 

Riyadh has yet to comment on the war, but it has grown closer to Eritrea in recent years, where its diplomatic engagement and investment has been encouraged by Egypt. 

The kingdom also backs the SAF in Sudan in its fight against the RSF, which in turn is supported by the UAE.

item.description:
Netanyahu pressed Qatar to continue funding Gaza despite security warnings, report finds

Submitted by Nadav Rapaport on Mon, 11/09/2026 - 14:49
Channel 12 investigation says Doha gave Israeli military and security officials gifts worth tens of thousands of shekels
Palestinians walk along a street lined with destroyed buildings at the Jabalia refugee camp in the northern Gaza Strip on 5 October 2026 (AFP)
Off

An Israeli Channel 12 News investigation has revealed that the Israeli government sought to ensure that Qatar continued transferring funds to the occupied Gaza Strip before 7 October 2023, despite warnings from security officials that the money was strengthening Hamas. 

The report details how Qatar became instrumental to Israel's policies in the besieged enclave over the past 15 years.

The policy, spearheaded by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu between 2011 and 2023, involved Qatari officials transferring tens of millions of US dollars in cash to the Gaza Strip in an effort to maintain stable relations between Israel and Hamas.

The investigation describes a process in which Israeli government and security officials asked Qatar to transfer the funds, while senior military officers reportedly received expensive gifts from Doha.

According to the report, the close connections between Qatar and Israel over Gaza were first discussed in 2011, during a secret meeting organised by then French President Nicolas Sarkozy.

Netanyahu and his Qatari counterpart Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani met at the Presidential Palace in Paris, where Al Thani offered his country's help in negotiating the release of Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit, who had been held captive by Hamas since 2006.

During the meeting, Al Thani also offered to transfer building materials, including cement and iron, to help rebuild the Palestinian enclave destroyed by Israeli bombardment.

Although Shalit was eventually released in late 2011 through Egyptian mediation, the Paris meeting was quickly followed by closer connection between the two countries, the report said. Israel allowed Qatari officials access to the Gaza Strip, while Qatar pledged to transfer $400m to the enclave in 2012.

Two years later, following the 2014 Gaza war, Israel's policy of involving Qatar in Gaza was further institutionalised, with Doha announcing a $1bn transfer to the war-ravaged Palestinian territory.

Suitcases of cash despite intelligence warnings

During those years, suitcases containing millions of dollars were delivered from Qatar to the Gaza Strip with the Israeli government's full approval, while the policy was kept secret, including from officials within Israel's security agencies.

Mohammed al-Emadi, Qatar's envoy to Gaza, was at the centre of these operations, developing close relationships with senior Israeli military officials over the years, the report said.

Emadi was tasked with delivering the suitcases of cash to Gaza, initially raising suspicions at Shin Bet, Israel's internal security agency. However, following a brief inquiry, the agency discovered that the transfers were being made with Netanyahu's approval.

Over the years, Netanyahu had several opportunities to end the transfer of Qatari funds to Gaza, which security officials warned were helping Hamas build its power. The Israeli prime minister, however, refused to do so, maintaining the policy until the outbreak of the Hamas-led 7 October attacks.

‘We do not want to die from the cold’: Gaza families struggle as rain floods shelters
Read More »

According to the report, Netanyahu rejected proposals by military officials to transfer the Qatari money to Gaza in Israeli shekels and through the Palestinian Authority, preferring instead for the funds to be delivered in dollars directly to Hamas.

Despite repeated warnings from security officials, Netanyahu ignored their concerns and continued to strengthen the connections between Israel and Qatar, the investigation indicated.

In 2020, when Qatar sought to stop the transfers, Netanyahu instructed then Mossad director Yossi Cohen to find an alternative source of funding.

Cohen reportedly met with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, then the ruler of Abu Dhabi and now the president of the UAE, asking them to replace Doha.

After both leaders refused, Cohen was sent to Qatar to persuade the emirate to continue transferring funds to Gaza.

Qatar ultimately continued the transfers until 2023. Over the years of his mission, the report said, the Qatari envoy to Gaza also gave gifts worth tens of thousands of shekels to officials in the Israeli army, Mossad and the National Security Council.

Effie Defrin, the current Israeli army spokesperson, received gifts from Qatar in 2022 while serving in another role in the army's Spokesperson's Unit, as did other senior officers, the report added.

The investigation concluded that Netanyahu and former prime minister Naftali Bennett continued the policy of transferring funds to Gaza despite warnings from security officials. It added that, just a week before the 7 October attacks, in which some 1,200 Israelis were killed and 250 taken captive by Hamas, Netanyahu instructed the Mossad to secure additional funding from Qatar.

item.description:
As heavy rains swamp Gaza's tents, Israel must face sanctions

It took a mere dozen hours of the first winter storm to flood around 70,000 tents in Gaza. Even 1,000 would be worthy of major humanitarian action, but just imagine that multiplied by 70.

These devastating floods were predicted and predictable. Nothing about this should surprise anyone who has paid even the scantest attention to the humanitarian situation in Gaza. 

Every year, Palestinians in the coastal enclave face the threat of flooding due to winter rains. Years ago, it was already challenging enough, as raw sewage flooded the streets, fuelling the spread of disease.

Israel’s blockade of Gaza, in place for two decades, along with periodic military bombardments, would render these inundations particularly life-threatening. Much of the debate in years past was about the inability to pump water out, including the lack of fuel for pumps, owing to Israel’s blockade. 

In contrast to the situation in 2026, however, that was a minor crisis.
